name: Infraorbital rim / zygomatic filler
lead: Infraorbital rim and zygomatic filler refers to injectable fillers, usually hyaluronic acid, placed around the lower orbital rim and cheekbone to add apparent support under the eye. Wikipedia describes injectable fillers as materials used to smooth wrinkles, restore volume and contour areas such as the cheeks [1]. In appearance communities the aim is often described as building skeletal-looking support for a deeper-set, more supported eye region. Hyaluronic acid itself is a natural polysaccharide first isolated from bovine eye tissue in 1934 and now a standard cosmetic filler material.[22]

The way it improves looks follows a direct chain: added volume over the cheekbone and under the orbital rim, then a smoother transition between lower lid and cheek, then a more rested, supported eye area and higher-looking cheekbones. Because hyaluronic acid filler is temporary, people also use it as a reversible trial run for the look that implants or surgery would give permanently.

The infraorbital area is anatomically delicate. Reviews list bruising, malar oedema, blue-grey discolouration and contour irregularities as common complications, with uncommon serious events [2]. Small pilot and cadaver studies have examined placement and behaviour of hyaluronic acid in the region [3][4], and manufacturers have registered trials of infraorbital filler products [9][10][11].

paras: Most hyaluronic acid fillers are chemically crosslinked, commonly with BDDE, to improve durability and resistance to enzymatic breakdown [1]. Infraorbital filler is used for tear trough and under-eye hollows; a 2024 paper notes ongoing debate about injection practice, placement depth and filler behaviour in this region [3].

Under-eye and cheek filler are often described together because the lower lid, the orbital rim and the cheek form one continuous contour. A cadaveric evaluation of filler in the tear trough and lid-cheek junction compared filler types and manipulation techniques [4], and clinicians describe the aim as blending the lower lid into the cheek rather than filling a single line.

Hyaluronic acid was first isolated in 1934 by Karl Meyer and John Palmer from the vitreous of a cow's eye, and the first HA biomedical product, the eye-surgery viscoelastic Healon, was developed by Pharmacia in the 1970s and 1980s.[22] Native HA has a short half-life, so cosmetic products are cross-linked, most often with BDDE, to extend duration; for facial wrinkles the effect lasts roughly 6 to 12 months.[22][1] HA is degraded by hyaluronidase enzymes.[22]

Cheek augmentation more broadly has three routes: solid implants (silicone, porous polyethylene or ePTFE) placed over the cheekbone through the mouth, injectable fillers such as hyaluronic acid or the patient's own fat, which are eventually absorbed, and rarely zygomatic osteotomy, a bone-cutting operation mostly used in reconstruction.[21] Implants are typically placed in one to two hours with recovery of about ten days, with risks of infection, bleeding, swelling, asymmetry and prolonged loss of sensation.[21]

On looksmax.org, members discuss filler alongside surgical options such as infraorbital rim and malar implants. One thread compares rim implants with malar implants, with a member arguing that off-the-shelf malar implants can give too much lower-face volume and that men need high, sharp cheekbones for which custom implants are the route [12]. Another thread shows a member planning cheek filler of about 1.5 ml per side to raise the cheeks and increase under-eye support, together with eyelid and smile-line filler [13].

Thread titles show the surrounding debate, including whether rim implants alone can lift the lower eyelids, whether they provide under-eye support, and how they differ from tear-trough implants [14][15][16]. Filler is described by some members as a cheaper and reversible preview of these changes; surgeons and published reviews describe filler and implant as different procedures with different risks.

A 2025 Clinics in Plastic Surgery review by Richard Warren describes the lower eyelid-cheek junction as a place where contour complaints usually trace to underlying anatomy: age-related bone loss leaves the infraorbital rim and maxilla recessed, and loss of cheek soft tissue contributes to tear trough deformity.[20] It groups tear troughs into three classes, each needing a different surgical approach, and notes that combined lower-lid and cheek procedures often give the greatest improvement.[20] This is the clinical logic behind treating rim and cheek together, and behind forum interest in rim and malar implants as permanent versions of the same idea.[20][12]

sections.h: Why the under-eye and cheek area is targeted
paras: Wikipedia's article on periorbital dark circles describes the lower eyelid as covered by very thin skin that accentuates features beneath it, including the bony rim and the orbicularis oculi muscle. [18] With age, it says, collagen is lost, facial fat descends and loses volume, and inflexible ligaments can produce hollowing at the orbital rim and cheek. [18] The shadow cast by a hollow can look like a dark circle even when the skin itself is not pigmented, which is the reasoning behind volume treatments for the area. [18]

The same article separates these structural causes from pigment and vascular causes, such as extra melanin or visible blood vessels under thin skin, and it lists hyaluronic acid fillers and autologous fat transplantation among options alongside creams, lasers and light-based treatments. [18] People who describe the look they are after as a more supported eye area are therefore generally describing a structural cause, which is the one filler and implants are meant to address. [18][12]

A 2024 CT study of 84 hemifacial specimens mapped infraorbital vasculature to inform safer injection [5]. A 2026 ultrasound study classified infraorbital fat and groove patterns, noting that placement into fat can cause bulging [6]. A review on the safety of injections in the infraorbital region discusses vessels and layers that clinicians use to choose depth [5].

sections.h: Filler compared with implants and fat
paras: Hyaluronic acid filler is temporary and is broken down over time, while rim and malar implants are surgical, solid, and intended to be permanent. [1][12] Wikipedia notes that fillers differ in how long they last, and describes autologous fat as another filling material, with embolic complications reported more often with fat than with hyaluronic acid. [1] Forum members often describe filler as a way of previewing how added cheek and rim projection would look on their own face before deciding on surgery, while surgeons and reviews treat the two as separate procedures with separate risk profiles. [12][13][2]

A 2020 review lists ecchymosis, malar oedema, blue-grey hue and contour irregularities as the most common complications of infraorbital filler [2]. Wikipedia reports that, rarely, filler can enter an artery and cause vascular occlusion, potentially leading to permanent vision loss or skin necrosis [1]. It adds that embolic complications are more common with autologous fat, followed by hyaluronic acid, and that vision loss, when it occurs, is usually permanent [1]. Other reported problems include infection, allergic reactions, lumps and scarring [1].

A 2024 CT study of 84 hemifacial specimens mapped infraorbital vasculature to inform safer injection [5], and a 2026 ultrasound study classified infraorbital fat and groove patterns, noting that placement into fat can cause bulging [6]. In the US, filler is regulated as a medical device that must be prescribed and injected by a provider; in the EU and UK it is a non-prescription device that needs a CE mark, which certifies production standards but not efficacy [1].

Small human and cadaver studies exist. A multimodal pilot study combined patient injections of a hyaluronic acid filler with 3D imaging, patient-reported outcomes and cadaveric assessment [3]. A completed registered study of infraorbital filler enrolled 11 participants [7], and a larger registry of real-life facial filler use (n=460) that includes cheek augmentation is recruiting [8].

A 2015 prospective, single-blind randomised study of 12 patients with tear trough deformity gave each hyaluronic acid filler in the tear trough on one side and the cheek on the other, then treated the remaining area. Three masked observers rated photographs: tear trough treatment alone significantly improved depth ratings (p = 0.0001), cheek-only treatment did not produce a significant change (p = 0.0963), and treating both areas did (p = 0.001). The authors reported that tear trough injection was more technique-sensitive and caused varying bruising, while cheek treatment caused no complications.[19]

Manufacturers have also registered controlled studies of infraorbital products: a phase 3 study of Volbella XC for infraorbital hollowing (n=163, completed) [9], a study of RHA Redensity Eye versus no treatment for infra-orbital hollows and tear-trough deformity (n=248, completed) [10], and a study of Teosyal RHA 1 in Chinese adults with infraorbital volume deficiency (n=260, recruiting) [11]. A further completed study measured satisfaction with periorbital aesthetics after Juvederm fillers and Botox (n=73) [17]. Results are not summarised here. Large controlled trials specific to rim or zygomatic augmentation for skeletal support were not found.

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, filler for the cheeks and under-eye area is discussed alongside infraorbital rim and malar implants as ways to build eye-area and cheekbone support [12][13].

claims.believers: A forum member plans about 1.5 ml of cheek filler per side to raise the cheeks and increase under-eye support [13].
claims.experts: Reviews describe infraorbital and cheek filler as adding volume, with studies examining placement and outcomes in small samples; larger registered trials are in progress [3][10].

claims.claim: Implants give men sharper cheekbones than off-the-shelf options or filler
claims.believers: A forum reply says men need high, sharp cheekbones and that custom implants are the only way, while off-the-shelf malar implants give too much lower-face volume [12].
claims.experts: No controlled studies compare filler and implants for this purpose in the studies found.

claims.claim: Under-eye filler carries risk because of the area's anatomy
claims.believers: Community threads frequently discuss surgeon choice for the area [14].
claims.experts: Reviews list common complications and rare vascular occlusion with vision loss; anatomical studies map vessels to refine placement [1][2][5].

claims.claim: Treating the cheek alone is enough to fix the under-eye hollow.
claims.believers: Forum members often pair cheek and rim augmentation to lift under-eye support and lower lids.[12][15]
claims.experts: In a 2015 randomised study of 12 patients, tear trough treatment improved depth ratings while cheek-only treatment did not reach significance.[19] A 2025 review says combined lid and cheek procedures often give the greatest improvement.[20]

card.summary: Hyaluronic acid filler placed around the under-eye rim and cheekbone for support; temporary, with a delicate and risky injection area.
card.aka: Tear trough filler, under-eye filler, cheek filler
card.note: Rare vascular occlusion can cause skin necrosis or permanent vision loss; common effects are bruising and swelling.

quick.overview:
Infraorbital rim and zygomatic filler uses injectable gel, usually hyaluronic acid, to add volume under the eye and over the cheekbone for a more supported look.

Evidence consists of small pilot studies, anatomical studies and complication reviews; no large trials were found.
quick.mechanism: Filler is injected into the tissue around the orbital rim and cheek to add volume and projection. Researchers are studying depth, vessel locations and fat patterns to refine placement [3][5][6].
quick.risks: Common effects are bruising, swelling, blue-grey tint and contour irregularities [2]. Rarely, filler entering an artery can cause tissue death or permanent vision loss [1]. Fillers are regulated as medical devices in the US [1].

chain: Gel placed along the orbital rim and over the cheekbone
Adds volume and projection under the eye
Smoother lid-cheek transition and fuller midface
angle.text: Hyaluronic acid gel adds volume where bone or fat is lacking under the eye and over the cheekbone, so the area looks more supported for as long as the filler lasts. Results are temporary and gradually fade as the body breaks the gel down.
